fact: AKC agility trial rules require a course area of at least 5,000 square feet for Novice, 6,500 for Open and 8,000 for Excellent, Master and Premier, at least 60 feet wide, and call a 100 by 120 foot ring ideal.
quote: The minimum usable course area must be 5,000 square feet for Novice, 6,500 square feet for Open, and 8,000 square feet for Excellent/Master/Premier. … While the previous square footage areas are the minimum sizes, a 100' x 120' ring is ideal for agility. … The course area must be moderately level and clear, and must be a minimum of 60-feet wide.
source_label: American Kennel Club, Regulations for Agility Trials and Agility Course Test (amended to January 3, 2024, with inserts effective August 1, 2024 and January 1, 2026)
notes: Chapter 4, Section 1. Read in full with curl and pdftotext on 2026-10-16. The two inserts change recording fees and ISC ribbons only; the ring, surface and obstacle sections are unchanged. AKC revisions often take effect January 1, so re-read after the 2027 rulebook or insert is out.

fact: AKC's Agility Course Test, an entry-level event for beginning dogs and handlers, needs a course area of at least 3,500 square feet (3,200 for its jumpers tests) and at least 40 feet wide.
quote: The Agility Course Test (ACT) is an entry level agility event to introduce beginning dogs and handlers to the sport of agility and the AKC agility program. … Must be a minimum useable course area must be 3500 square feet for ACT1 and ACT2. For ACT1J and ACT2J the minimum useable course area must be 3200 square feet. The course area must be moderately level and clear,and be a minimum of 40 feet wide.
source_label: American Kennel Club, Regulations for Agility Trials and Agility Course Test (amended to January 3, 2024, with inserts effective August 1, 2024 and January 1, 2026)
notes: Chapter 15, Sections 1 and 9. The rulebook's own wording, typos included ("Must be a minimum useable course area must be", "clear,and").

fact: AKC recommends 15 to 18 feet between obstacles, at least 18 feet to a jump and 21 feet to a spread jump, and no more than 30 feet between two obstacles in sequence, measured along the path of a dog jumping 20 inches.
quote: It is recommended that there be a minimum of 15 feet to 18 feet between obstacles, with a minimum of 18 feet to a jump, 21 feet to a spread jump, and a maximum of 30 feet between any two obstacles in sequence as measured along the anticipated path of a 20 inch high jumping dog.
source_label: American Kennel Club, Regulations for Agility Trials and Agility Course Test (amended to January 3, 2024, with inserts effective August 1, 2024 and January 1, 2026)
notes: Chapter 4, Section 4.

fact: AKC requires agility courses on non-slip surfaces, names packed dirt, grass, carpeting and padded matting as acceptable, requires concrete to be fully matted or padded, and limits how sharply a course turns into an obstacle with the running surface in mind.
quote: Courses must be set up on non-slip surfaces, whether indoors or outdoors (packed dirt, grass, carpeting and padded matting are acceptable surfaces). If a course is run on concrete, the area must be fully matted or padded. … Approach angles to obstacles shall not exceed the following, with additional consideration for safety, based on the obstacle being approached and the running surface.
source_label: American Kennel Club, Regulations for Agility Trials and Agility Course Test (amended to January 3, 2024, with inserts effective August 1, 2024 and January 1, 2026)
notes: Chapter 4, Sections 2 and 5. The parenthetical names those four surfaces; it does not mention artificial turf either way, so a page must not say AKC allows or bars turf.

fact: AKC's regular agility classes set jump height by the dog's height at the withers: 8 inches for dogs 11 inches and under, 12 for 14 and under, 16 for 18 and under, 20 for 22 and under, and 24 for dogs over 22 inches.
quote: 8 Inches: For dogs 11 inches and under at the withers. 12 Inches: For dogs 14 inches and under at the withers. 16 Inches: For dogs 18 inches and under at the withers. 20 Inches: For dogs 22 inches and under at the withers. 24 Inches: For dogs over 22 inches at the withers.
source_label: American Kennel Club, Regulations for Agility Trials and Agility Course Test (amended to January 3, 2024, with inserts effective August 1, 2024 and January 1, 2026)
notes: Chapter 2, Section 4 (Regular classes). Preferred classes jump 4 inches lower (Chapter 8, Section 9); a 24 Inch Choice option also exists.

fact: AKC requires jump uprights that can be knocked over and bars 4 to 5 feet long that sit loose on their supports so a dog can knock them off.
quote: Bar Jumps consist of bars that are supported by bar supports that are mounted to uprights. Uprights must be displaceable. … can be made from Schedule 40 PVC or Schedule 40 furniture grade PVC, 4 to 5 feet long and striped for visibility. … The bottom of the bar sits on top of the bar supports such that the bar is easily displaced.
source_label: American Kennel Club, Regulations for Agility Trials and Agility Course Test (amended to January 3, 2024, with inserts effective August 1, 2024 and January 1, 2026)
notes: Chapter 3, Section 3, item 7.

fact: AKC weave poles are 40 inches tall and spaced 24 inches center to center, on a non-slip base no higher than three-quarters of an inch and no wider than three and a half inches, secured so the poles don't move.
quote: The base shall be coated with a non-slip surface and may be no higher than ¾-inch and no wider than 3½-inches. The base should be secured, so that the weave poles do not move from their location on the course. … 40 inches in height, and uniformly spaced at 24 inches (measured center to center using two of the rigid upright supports, with a +/- ½-inch tolerance in spacing).
source_label: American Kennel Club, Regulations for Agility Trials and Agility Course Test (amended to January 3, 2024, with inserts effective August 1, 2024 and January 1, 2026)
notes: Chapter 3, Section 3, item 6.

fact: AKC's open tunnel has round openings 25 inches across, give or take 2, runs 10 to 20 feet, and must be secured so a dog can't move it, with no holder under it more than an inch and a half thick and no rigid upright that could poke between the ribs.
quote: The two openings are round with a height and width of 25 inches plus or minus (+/-) 2 inches with 4-inch rib spacing required. Its length is 10 to 20 feet and it is secured in position to prevent a dog from moving it. No portion of a tunnel holder that is underneath the tunnel shall be more than 1½-inches thick and the tunnel supports shall not have a rigid upright (i.e., steel/wood) that is capable of fitting between the ribs thus possibly projecting into the tunnel.
source_label: American Kennel Club, Regulations for Agility Trials and Agility Course Test (amended to January 3, 2024, with inserts effective August 1, 2024 and January 1, 2026)
notes: Chapter 3, Section 3, item 5. A page number (36) falls mid-sentence in the PDF and is left out.

fact: AKC agility trials are open to dogs 15 months of age or older.
quote: Section 3. Eligibility of Dogs. All dogs fifteen (15) months of age or older that are registered with the American Kennel Club …
source_label: American Kennel Club, Regulations for Agility Trials and Agility Course Test (amended to January 3, 2024, with inserts effective August 1, 2024 and January 1, 2026)
notes: Chapter 1, Section 3. The ACT has the same 15-month floor (Chapter 15, Section 3). An eligibility rule, not veterinary advice on when a young dog may jump.

fact: USDAA's at-home agility program is built for individual or small-group runs: its full courses are generally 60 by 80 feet or larger, its small courses smaller, and its skills-test courses any size.
quote: This platform provides courses engineered for individual or small group participation in a less formal setting than provided at “live” events. … Courses generally 60’ x 80’ or larger, including a mix of challenges … Courses generally 60’ x 80’ or smaller, including a mix of challenges with fewer course segments than a full course … Any size, including skills involving obstacle focus, direction/distance control, and/or handler positioning
source_label: USDAA, USDAA@Home! Rules & Regulations for Dog Agility (as adopted October 1, 2024)
notes: The three course descriptions are the Full Course, Small Course and Skills Test Course rows of the point-value table. Summary of Chapter 13 of the USDAA Rules & Regulations, which is not posted as a separate file we could open.

fact: For its at-home courses, USDAA accepts weave poles of pipe up to 1 inch thick and 36 inches tall stuck in the ground in a straight line 24 inches apart, and a pause box on the ground no more than 4 feet square in place of a table.
quote: May be poles or pipe up to 1” diameter x 36” tall, stuck in the ground on a straight line with 24” spacing … A pause box on the ground, with identifiable lines, no more than 4’ square (e.g., a 4’ x 4’ nonslip mat, a place on the ground with sides or corners marked.) For a pause box, the dog must have all four feet in the box for the five-second count
source_label: USDAA, USDAA@Home! Required Dog Agility Obstacles & Allowable Substitutions (last updated October 1, 2025)
notes: Weave Poles and Table rows of the substitutions table; allowed only for USDAA@Home! courses.

fact: NADAC, which sanctions agility events, requires weave poles 24 inches apart on a base no more than half an inch high, with offset support legs 12 to 18 inches long and enough weight to stay put without stakes, and does not allow staking at its events.
quote: The poles are required to be 24” spacing, measured from the center of one pole to the center of the next pole. The base of the weave poles shall be no more than 1/2” in height. … The support legs should be offset so that the dog’s path never crosses over a support leg and are to be of sufficient length (12-18”) to support the poles without staking. The sets of weave poles should be of sufficient weight as to not need staking to remain in place. Staking of weave poles is not allowed for NADAC Sanctioned events or VT’s.
source_label: NADAC, Equipment Specifications and Recommendations (January 15, 2025)

fact: NADAC recommends saddle-bag tunnel holders with at least 20 pounds of sand or 3 gallons of water in each, requires 4 bags on a 15-foot tunnel and 5 on a 20-foot one, and bars bungee cords, chains and metal cradles.
quote: NADAC recommends “saddle bag” type tunnel holders be used for all NADAC classes. At Least 20 pounds of sand or 3 gallons of water, in each bag, has proven to be sufficient to hold tunnels in place. Note: If sand is used, it is recommended that it be dispersed into individual zip lock baggies and then inserted into the tunnel bag. … Bungee cords or chains are not allowed. Metal “cradle” type tunnel holders are not allowed. … 15’ Tunnels: 4 bags are required. They should be spaced evenly throughout the tunnel. 20’ Tunnels: 5 Bags are required.
source_label: NADAC, Equipment Specifications and Recommendations (January 15, 2025)

fact: NADAC wants jumps made of plastic or PVC, with individual plastic stanchions, so that a jump a dog hits falls easily without injuring it.
quote: As of June 1, 2023: Jumps should be made of all Plastic/PVC. … NADAC recommends the use of individual jump stanchions constructed out of plastic. This is to ensure that if a dog collides with a jump, it falls easily without causing injury.
source_label: NADAC, Equipment Specifications and Recommendations (January 15, 2025)

fact: NADAC says contact obstacles need a non-slip surface with good traction that is not so rough it damages a dog's pads, maintained so dogs don't slip.
quote: Contact obstacles should always have a non-slip surface that provides good traction for the dogs without being so rough as to damage the dog’s pads. Surfaces must be maintained on a regular basis to ensure that dogs will not slip or injure themselves when performing these obstacles.
source_label: NADAC, Equipment Specifications and Recommendations (January 15, 2025)
notes: Written for contact obstacles (A-frame, dog walk), not for the ground; a page may use it only as NADAC's standard for those obstacles.

fact: In a 2022 survey of the handlers of 308 agility dogs by veterinary sports-medicine researchers, half the dogs (50.8%) trained on artificial turf, second only to grass (85.3%), and handlers saw the fewest signs of poor performance on grass and dirt.
quote: In this retrospective, cross-sectional study, 300 respondents (handlers, owners, and trainers) of 308 agility dogs completed an online survey … Dogs most commonly trained on natural grass (85.3%), artificial turf (50.8%), and dirt (34.5%). Significantly fewer MDPs were observed on natural grass than any other substrate except dirt. … Overall, agility dogs were perceived to perform best on natural grass and dirt, while rubber mat was associated with injury and decreased performance.
source_label: Jimenez, Canapp and Percival, Internet-based survey evaluating the impact of ground substrate on injury and performance in canine agility athletes, Frontiers in Veterinary Science (2022)
notes: MDPs = markers of decreased performance. Authors from the Veterinary Orthopedic and Sports Medicine Group and Canapp Sports Medicine (co-founded by author Sherman Canapp), plus a Clean Run Magazine employee; conflicts are declared in the paper. Handler perception, cross-sectional.

fact: The same researchers write that a stiffer floor absorbs less energy and sends more force back into a dog's body, while a good one grips for turns and takeoffs and cushions the landing after a jump.
quote: Substrate composition and quality may influence the risk of slips, falls, or other injuries associated with agility. Stiffer (less compliant) flooring absorbs less energy, thus transferring more force back into the dog's musculoskeletal structures … Conversely, a high-quality floor provides good traction for turns and jump-offs and acts as a shock absorber for landing after a jump.
source_label: Jimenez, Canapp and Percival, Internet-based survey evaluating the impact of ground substrate on injury and performance in canine agility athletes, Frontiers in Veterinary Science (2022)
notes: Introduction; the ellipsis replaces the citation numbers.

fact: The researchers picture a dog on a running turn on artificial turf with the toes of its inside front leg bent back past straight, note that front-toe injuries are common in agility dogs, and say turf may need its infill topped up over time.
quote: (F) A dog takes a running turn on artificial turf, demonstrating hyperextension of the digits of the inside forelimb. Forelimb digit injuries are common in agility dogs. Artificial turf may require replenishment of infill over time, and filling types appear to influence the rate of injury in prior literature.
source_label: Jimenez, Canapp and Percival, Internet-based survey evaluating the impact of ground substrate on injury and performance in canine agility athletes, Frontiers in Veterinary Science (2022)
notes: Figure 1, panel F caption. The "prior literature" on filling types is the Finnish survey (see inkila-infill-shares), whose own figures track how often each surface was used.

fact: About a quarter of the competition injuries in that survey happened on grass and about a quarter on turf, but handlers blamed the surface for 42.9% of the turf injuries against about a quarter of the grass ones, and the authors caution that a perceived link does not prove the surface caused an injury.
quote: For example, approximately a quarter of CIs occurred on both natural grass and artificial turf. However, while only a quarter of CI sustained on natural grass were perceived to be secondary to the substrate, artificial turf was perceived to be responsible for 42.9% of CI on that substrate. … A perceived association between injury and substrate does not confirm that the injury was caused by the substrate
source_label: Jimenez, Canapp and Percival, Internet-based survey evaluating the impact of ground substrate on injury and performance in canine agility athletes, Frontiers in Veterinary Science (2022)
notes: CI = competition injury. Discussion section.

fact: Of the dogs that trained on rubber mat, 32.0% were hurt in training on it, the highest rate of any surface, against 3.77% of dogs that trained on dirt, and handlers blamed rubber mat in 87.5% of the training injuries that happened on it.
quote: Rubber mat had the highest IP (32.0% [16/50]) while dirt had the lowest IP (3.77% [4/106]) … Rubber mat was the substrate most often perceived by respondents to be responsible for the injury (87.5%)
source_label: Jimenez, Canapp and Percival, Internet-based survey evaluating the impact of ground substrate on injury and performance in canine agility athletes, Frontiers in Veterinary Science (2022)
notes: IP = incidence proportion: dogs injured in training on a surface over dogs that trained on it. Results section.

fact: Handlers in that survey most often linked training injuries to jumps (37.5%) and contact obstacles (29.7%), and linked 25.0% of competition injuries to tunnels.
quote: Obstacles perceived to be associated with injuries included jumps (TI: 37.5%, CI: 27.8%), contacts (TI: 29.7%, CI: 22.2%), weaves (TI: 11.9%, CI: 13.9%), and tunnels (CI: 25.0%).
source_label: Jimenez, Canapp and Percival, Internet-based survey evaluating the impact of ground substrate on injury and performance in canine agility athletes, Frontiers in Veterinary Science (2022)
notes: Abstract. TI = training injury, CI = competition injury.

fact: In a University of Helsinki survey of 864 Finnish competition agility dogs, slipping was part of 42.3% of the injuries that happened on an obstacle, but the type of field surface was not associated with slipping.
quote: A retrospective online questionnaire was used to collect data on 864 Finnish competition-level agility dogs … Of obstacle-related injuries, slipping during obstacle performance had occurred in 42.3% (22/52) of dogs. … field surface was not associated with slipping in the same regression model (p = 0.517).
source_label: Inkilä et al., Part II of Finnish Agility Dog Survey: Agility-Related Injuries and Risk Factors for Injury in Competition-Level Agility Dogs, Animals (2022)
notes: Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, University of Helsinki, with the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences. Surfaces in the study were mostly artificial turf (with rubber, cork, sand or no filling) and dirt or sand.

fact: Two-thirds of the injured Finnish dogs (67.6%) were hurt on a surface they had trained or competed on every week for the three months before.
quote: Two-thirds (67.6%; 75/111) of the dogs injured themselves on a familiar surface on which they had trained or competed on a weekly basis during the three-month period prior to the injury.
source_label: Inkilä et al., Part II of Finnish Agility Dog Survey: Agility-Related Injuries and Risk Factors for Injury in Competition-Level Agility Dogs, Animals (2022)

fact: Among the injured Finnish dogs, 35.1% were hurt on turf with rubber infill and 12.6% on turf with cork infill, close to the 32.5% and 12.0% of those dogs that trained and competed mainly on each.
quote: Artificial turf with rubber filling 39/111 35.1% … Artificial turf with cork filling 14/111 12.6% … The main surfaces used in training and competition during the preceding three months included artificial turf with rubber (32.5%; 38/117), dirt or sand (26.5%; 31/117), artificial turf without filling (21.4%; 25/117), artificial turf with cork filling (12.0%; 14/117)
source_label: Inkilä et al., Part II of Finnish Agility Dog Survey: Agility-Related Injuries and Risk Factors for Injury in Competition-Level Agility Dogs, Animals (2022)
notes: First two parts are rows of Table 4 (field surface at the time of injury, n = 111), cells joined; the last part is section 3.4.3 (injured dogs' main surface in the three months before injury). The comparison of the two is ours, from the paper's own figures.

fact: The Finnish researchers found open-tunnel injuries more common than earlier studies had, suggested that faster dogs, grippier tunnel material and more fixed tunnel attachments may have raised the hazard, found collisions most common at jumps, and said lightweight obstacles reduce the impact when a dog hits one.
quote: Interestingly, in addition to these obstacles, injuries during performance of open tunnels were relatively common in our study, whereas previously open tunnels have only seldom been associated with injuries … Observations from the field suggest that the speed of the dogs has increased over the years, materials of tunnels have evolved to improve the grip for the dog, and the attachments of tunnels has become more fixed … possibly increasing the hazards of open tunnels. … In our study, collisions were particularly common on jump obstacles compared with other obstacles … Attention should be paid to materials of obstacles; lightweight obstacles are going to reduce the impact to the dog in the case of collision with the obstacle.
source_label: Inkilä et al., Part II of Finnish Agility Dog Survey: Agility-Related Injuries and Risk Factors for Injury in Competition-Level Agility Dogs, Animals (2022)
notes: Discussion section; ellipses mark skipped citations and text.

fact: More than two agility training sessions a week was among the factors more common in the injured Finnish dogs, and the researchers note that such associations do not prove cause.
quote: Other common factors among the injured dogs included older age when starting course-like training and more than two agility-training sessions a week. … These associations do not confirm causality.
source_label: Inkilä et al., Part II of Finnish Agility Dog Survey: Agility-Related Injuries and Risk Factors for Injury in Competition-Level Agility Dogs, Animals (2022)
notes: Simple Summary, then Abstract.

fact: Front paw pads were among the injured locations in 5.9% of the injured Finnish dogs.
quote: Additional injured anatomical locations included paw pad (front limb) (5.9%; 7/119)
source_label: Inkilä et al., Part II of Finnish Agility Dog Survey: Agility-Related Injuries and Risk Factors for Injury in Competition-Level Agility Dogs, Animals (2022)
notes: Section 3.3.1. The paper does not say what caused the pad injuries.

fact: A study of UK veterinary records for over 900,000 dogs found exercise was the most common trigger of heat-related illness, 74.2% of events with a known cause, that heatstroke from exercise was as likely to kill as heatstroke in a hot car, and that young, male and flat-faced dogs had higher odds of it.
quote: We reviewed the veterinary records of over 900,000 dogs and identified that exercise was the most common trigger of heat-related illness in dogs. We also found that heatstroke caused by exercise was just as likely to kill as heatstroke from a hot car. Male dogs and younger dogs were more likely to develop heat-related illnesses triggered by exercise. … the predominant trigger of HRI presenting to UK primary-care practices was exertional HRI (74.2% of events with a known cause). … brachycephalic dogs had increased odds of exertional HRI when compared to mesocephalic dogs.
source_label: Hall, Carter and O'Neill, Dogs Don't Die Just in Hot Cars: Exertional Heat-Related Illness (Heatstroke) Is a Greater Threat to UK Dogs, Animals (2020)
notes: VetCompass primary-care records for 2016 (Royal Veterinary College). Simple Summary, then Discussion. HRI = heat-related illness; brachycephalic = flat-faced.

fact: NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals average 58.3 days a year at or above 90°F at Greeley UNC, 48.8 at Longmont 2 ESE and 29.5 at Fort Collins, with June to August average highs of 88.9°F, 87.5°F and 84.7°F.
quote: {"STATION":"USC00053553","ANN-TMAX-AVGNDS-GRTH090":"    58.3","JJA-TMAX-NORMAL":"    88.9","NAME":"GREELEY UNC, CO US"} … {"STATION":"USC00053005","ANN-TMAX-AVGNDS-GRTH090":"    29.5","JJA-TMAX-NORMAL":"    84.7","NAME":"FT COLLINS, CO US"} … {"STATION":"USC00055116","ANN-TMAX-AVGNDS-GRTH090":"    48.8","JJA-TMAX-NORMAL":"    87.5","NAME":"LONGMONT 2 ESE, CO US"}
source_label: NOAA NCEI U.S. Climate Normals 1991 to 2020, annual/seasonal, stations GREELEY UNC (USC00053553), FT COLLINS (USC00053005) and LONGMONT 2 ESE (USC00055116)
notes: ANN-TMAX-AVGNDS-GRTH090 = average days a year with a high at or above 90°F; JJA-TMAX-NORMAL = June to August average high. Fixed until NOAA publishes the 2001 to 2030 normals. Station-to-town assignment is by proximity; say "the nearest NOAA station".

fact: The Motz Group, which sells turf infill and shock pads, describes a shock pad as foam between the base and the turf, sells pads 0.47 to 2.125 inches thick of closed-cell foam that lets water pass through and absorbs none, says a non-absorbing pad is essentially required with a dog, and says a pad on a solid base makes the surface evenly stable.
quote: A shock pad is a middle layer of padding installed between the sub-base layer and the layer of artificial turf. Shock pads (not to be confused with rigid, plastic drainage layers) are made from different types of foam with varying thicknesses. Our pads vary in thickness between 0.47 inches and 2.125 inches and are designed to let water pass vertically. All of the pads offered by Motz are made from closed-cell foam and do not absorb moisture. Non-absorbing pads are essentially required if you have a dog. … Shock pads installed on a solid base make an artificial turf surface uniformly stable throughout the lawn or playground, regardless of temperature and weather conditions.
source_label: The Motz Group, Why Use a Shock Pad? (Dec. 14, 2016, modified Jan. 27, 2023)
notes: A seller's blog; its pad claims are the maker's, not test results. The post's fall-height and concussion claims are about children and are not used.

fact: ForeverLawn sells K9Grass Sport, a dog turf with a 1 1/2 inch blade for canine athletic competition, with infill it calls optional and adjustable to the traction wanted, and says the product is designed to reduce the risk of injury.
quote: K9Grass Sport is a superior surfacing solution for canine athletic competition. … BLADE HEIGHT 1 1/2” … INFILL Optional & adjustable to desired traction level … infill in K9Grass Sport can be adjusted based on the specific needs of each application. … designed to reduce risk of injury.
source_label: ForeverLawn, K9Grass Sport product sheet (M1816 Rev. 1/25)
notes: A maker's sheet; "designed to reduce risk of injury" is the maker's claim, with no test cited on the sheet. The sheet also lists a 48 oz face weight and a warranty term, not used. A page names it as a published example, not a recommendation.

fact: EcoGrass, a turf company, says to set a stake through turf by parting the blades, cutting a small X in the backing between rows, keeping sharp edges below the surface, and plugging the holes when nothing is in them.
quote: To insert an anchor or stake into turf, locate the area where you'll install it, then gently spread the turf blades to expose the backing. Cut a small X in the backing, being careful not to damage the visible grass blades. … Look for areas between the rows of artificial grass blades to minimize damage. … Check that no sharp edges are exposed above the turf surface. Cover any protruding anchor heads with rubber caps or infill material to prevent trips and injuries. … When not in use, cover anchor holes in artificial turf with plugs to keep out debris and maintain appearance.
source_label: EcoGrass, Inserting Anchor or Stake into Turf (Shahe Sandjian, Aug. 7, 2024)
notes: A turf seller's how-to written for swing-set anchors and edges; a page applies it to stick-in poles as general practice, not as EcoGrass's agility advice.
